# Worksheet: adding a latent period

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../../chapters/04-jump-processes.qmd) simulated an SIR epidemic as an
exact sequence of events: draw a waiting time, pick which event fires, update the
state, repeat. Here you keep
that machinery and change the *disease*. Many infections have a **latent
period**, someone infected but not yet infectious, which adds a fourth
compartment $E$ and a third transition.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Parts A and B are the session.** **Part C** goes further if you get there; not
reaching it is fine. Worked solutions are posted at the end of each
day. Run `git pull` to collect them.

[Julia essentials worksheet](../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd)
opens with an R-to-Julia table, and a reminder of how to type `κ`, `σ` and `γ`.
The [Julia essentials chapter](../../prerequisites/01-julia-essentials.qmd) has

## Setup

Run this and check `R₀` prints as 2.0. The `gillespie` function is the session's
loop, written once so it can drive any model you hand it.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-setup
using CairoMakie
using Random
using StableRNGs
using Statistics

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

# `propensities(u, p)` returns one rate per transition, and column j of
# `stoichiometry` is what transition j does to the state.
function gillespie(u0, p, tmax, propensities, stoichiometry, rng)
    u = collect(u0)
    t = 0.0
    ts, us = [t], [copy(u)]
    while true
        a = propensities(u, p)
        a₀ = sum(a)
        a₀ == 0 && break                 # no transition can fire: absorbed
        t += randexp(rng) / a₀           # τ ~ Exponential(a₀)
        t > tmax && break
        target = rand(rng) * a₀          # pick j with probability aⱼ / a₀
        j = something(findfirst(≥(target), cumsum(a)), length(a))
        u .+= stoichiometry[:, j]
        push!(ts, t); push!(us, copy(u))
    end
    return ts, us
end

sample_states(ts, us, grid) =
    reduce(hcat, (us[searchsortedlast(ts, t)] for t in grid))

κ = 0.05 * 10 / 1000     # β c / N, as in the session
σ = 0.5                  # progression rate: mean latent period 1/σ = 2 days
γ = 0.25                 # recovery rate
grid = 0.0:0.5:120.0

println("R₀ = ", 0.05 * 10 / γ)
```

---

## Part A — an exposed compartment (~15 min)

The disease now has three transitions rather than two:

| transition | who moves | propensity |
|---|---|---|
| infection | $S \to E$ | $\kappa SI$ |
| progression | $E \to I$ | $\sigma E$ |
| recovery | $I \to R$ | $\gamma I$ |

You supply two things: what each transition does to the new $E$ compartment, and
the three propensities, in the same order as the columns.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-a1
# Column j says what transition j does to (S, E, I, R).
#           infection  progression  recovery
seir_stoichiometry = [
    -1   0   0     # S
     0   0   0     # E   TODO: replace this row — what does each transition do to E?
     0   1  -1     # I
     0   0   1     # R
]

function seir_propensities(u, p)
    S, E, I, R = u
    κ, σ, γ = p
    return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]   # TODO: replace the three zeros with the rates above
end

seir_u0 = (990, 0, 10, 0)
seir_p = (κ, σ, γ)
ts, us = gillespie(seir_u0, seir_p, last(grid), seir_propensities,
                   seir_stoichiometry, StableRNG(1))
path = sample_states(ts, us, grid)

check("population conserved", all(sum(path; dims = 1) .== 1000))
check("nobody went negative", minimum(path) >= 0)
check("the exposed compartment is used", maximum(path[2, :]) > 0)
check("an epidemic happened", path[4, end] > 100)
println("events = ", length(ts) - 1, ", peak infectious = ", maximum(path[3, :]))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A

```julia
     1  -1   0     # E
...
return [κ * S * I, σ * E, γ * I]
```

Read the $E$ row across the three transitions: infection puts someone *into* $E$
($+1$), progression takes them *out* ($-1$), and recovery does not touch $E$
($0$). Every column should sum to zero: nobody is created or destroyed.

If the conservation check fails, the $E$ row is the place to look. If nothing
happens at all (zero events, no epidemic), you have probably written
`κ * S * E` for the first rate. Infection needs someone *infectious* to do the
infecting, and people in $E$ are not yet infectious.
:::

### The same model, in three lines

Nothing to fill in here: read it and run it. This is the library half of the
session: the model you just specified as a $4\times3$ matrix plus a propensity
function, written as three reactions. In the first reaction $I$ appears on both
sides because an infectious person is unchanged by infecting someone else; the
transition moves one person from $S$ to $E$. Catalyst reads $\kappa$ as a
mass-action rate constant, so that reaction's propensity is $\kappa SI$, the
same expression you wrote by hand.

The two implementations are the same stochastic process but consume randomness
differently, so identical seeds do not give identical paths and only their
distributions can be compared. The cell therefore runs 20 of each and asks
whether the mean peaks differ by more than three standard errors of that
difference, the comparison from the session's recap slide. Passing means no
difference was detected at that resolution, not that the two are proven
identical.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-a2
using Catalyst
using JumpProcesses

seir_network = @reaction_network begin
    κ, S + I --> E + I
    σ, E --> I
    γ, I --> R
end

# Species are named, not positional: ask for `seir_network.I` rather than row 3.
function network_peak(seed)
    problem = JumpProblem(seir_network,
                          [:S => 990, :E => 0, :I => 10, :R => 0],
                          (0.0, last(grid)), [:κ => κ, :σ => σ, :γ => γ];
                          aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed))
    return maximum(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = grid)[seir_network.I])
end

function hand_peak(seed)
    ts, us = gillespie(seir_u0, seir_p, last(grid), seir_propensities,
                       seir_stoichiometry, StableRNG(seed))
    return maximum(sample_states(ts, us, grid)[3, :])
end

M = 20
network_peaks = [network_peak(2000 + k) for k in 1:M]
hand_peaks = [hand_peak(3000 + k) for k in 1:M]

# Standard error of the difference between two independent ensemble means.
standard_error = sqrt((var(network_peaks) + var(hand_peaks)) / M)

check("your model and the reaction network agree on the mean peak",
      abs(mean(network_peaks) - mean(hand_peaks)) < 3 * standard_error)
println("mean peak infectious: network ", round(mean(network_peaks); digits = 1),
        ", yours ", round(mean(hand_peaks); digits = 1),
        " (standard error of the difference ",
        round(standard_error; digits = 1), ")")
```

This check compares your Part A model with the reaction network, so it stays ✗
until the stoichiometry row and the propensities above are right.

### A1. Interpret

Why is the first propensity a product of two compartments while the other two
depend on only one?

Then compare the two specifications you now have of one model. Which parts of
the $4\times3$ matrix are hard to get right by hand, and what does the reaction
network make impossible to get wrong?

## Part B — does the latent period matter? (~15 min)

Below, the same machinery runs the session's SIR model so the two can be
compared. Both have $R_0 = 2$.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-b1
function sir_propensities(u, p)
    S, I, R = u
    κ, γ = p
    return [κ * S * I, γ * I]
end
sir_stoichiometry = [-1 0; 1 -1; 0 1]

function ensemble(u0, p, propensities, stoichiometry, M, seed0)
    return cat((sample_states(
                    gillespie(u0, p, last(grid), propensities,
                              stoichiometry, StableRNG(seed0 + k))...,
                    grid) for k in 1:M)...; dims = 3)
end

M = 30
seir_runs = ensemble(seir_u0, seir_p, seir_propensities, seir_stoichiometry, M, 100)
sir_runs  = ensemble((990, 10, 0), (κ, γ), sir_propensities, sir_stoichiometry, M, 200)

seir_I = dropdims(mean(seir_runs[3, :, :]; dims = 2), dims = 2)
sir_I  = dropdims(mean(sir_runs[2, :, :]; dims = 2), dims = 2)

seir_final = mean(seir_runs[4, end, :])
sir_final  = mean(sir_runs[3, end, :])

check("the SEIR peak comes later", grid[argmax(seir_I)] > grid[argmax(sir_I)])
check("the SEIR peak is lower", maximum(seir_I) < maximum(sir_I))
check("both reach a similar final size",
      abs(seir_final - sir_final) / sir_final < 0.05)
(; seir_peak_day = grid[argmax(seir_I)], sir_peak_day = grid[argmax(sir_I)],
   seir_peak = round(maximum(seir_I); digits = 1),
   sir_peak = round(maximum(sir_I); digits = 1),
   seir_final = round(seir_final; digits = 1),
   sir_final = round(sir_final; digits = 1))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch04-compare
#| fig-cap: "Mean infectious curve over 30 exact simulations, with and without a latent period."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 400))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time (days)", ylabel = "mean infectious")
lines!(ax, grid, sir_I; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 3, label = "SIR")
lines!(ax, grid, seir_I; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 3, label = "SEIR")
xlims!(ax, 0, 70)
axislegend(ax; position = :rt)
fig
```

### B1. Interpret

- Approximately when does each epidemic peak, and roughly how much lower is the
  SEIR peak?
- Both models end with about the same number of people ever infected, but the
  curves look very different. What does the latent period change, and what does
  it leave alone?

> *Your answer here.*

### B2. Experiment

Try a shorter and a longer latent period either side of the baseline
$\sigma = 0.5$, and watch the peak move.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-b2
latent_rates = Float64[]   # TODO: fill this list — try σ = 1.0, 0.5, and 0.25

for s in latent_rates
    runs = ensemble(seir_u0, (κ, s, γ), seir_propensities, seir_stoichiometry, 10, 300)
    mean_I = dropdims(mean(runs[3, :, :]; dims = 2), dims = 2)
    println("mean latent period ", round(1 / s; digits = 1), " days → peak on day ",
            grid[argmax(mean_I)])
end

check("three latent periods tried", length(latent_rates) == 3)
```

Does doubling the latent period move the peak by twice as much, or by more?

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — how often does an outbreak fizzle out? (optional)

*Start this only if you have finished Part B.*

Every simulation so far began with 10 infectious people and every one produced
an epidemic. Real introductions are usually a single case, and many single cases
infect nobody. A deterministic model cannot describe this at all; an exact
event simulation can.

The quantity to compare against is $1/R_0$, but be clear about where it comes
from. While cases are few the susceptible pool is essentially undepleted, so an
infectious individual infects at rate $\beta c$ and recovers at rate $\gamma$:
a linear birth–death process. Because infectious lifetimes are exponential
here, its extinction probability is $q = \gamma/(\beta c) = 1/R_0$ when
$R_0 > 1$. That formula belongs to this approximation; it is not universal
across branching processes or infectious-period distributions.

Two further approximations separate it from what the code measures. This model
has 999 susceptibles, not infinitely many, and the code below scores an outbreak
as faded if fewer than 20 people were ever infected rather than asking whether
transmission truly stopped. The run is a check on how good an approximation
$1/R_0$ is here.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch04-c1
function fades_out(seed)
    start = (990, 0, 10, 0)   # TODO: replace this — start from a single infectious individual
    ts, us = gillespie(start, seir_p, last(grid), seir_propensities,
                       seir_stoichiometry, StableRNG(seed))
    # Outcomes are bimodal: a handful of cases, or hundreds. Any cut between the
    # two modes gives the same answer, so 20 is not a delicate choice.
    return last(us)[4] < 20
end

trials = 400
fade_fraction = count(fades_out, 1:trials) / trials
predicted = γ / (0.05 * 10)   # 1 / R₀, the branching-process approximation

check("fade-out is close to the branching prediction",
      abs(fade_fraction - predicted) < 0.05)
(; fade_fraction, predicted)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C

```julia
start = (999, 0, 1, 0)
```

Keep the population at 1000: one infectious individual means 999 susceptible
ones. If the fraction comes out near zero, check you did not leave 10 infectious
people in the starting state.
:::

### C1. Interpret

- What fraction of outbreaks died out, and how does it compare with $1/R_0$?
- The deterministic model, started from one case, predicts a certain epidemic
  every time. Why can it not produce the answer you just measured?
